At nearly 100 meters high, its dome is worth the climb (or take the elevator) for a 360-degree view, including the Castle District and Parliament on either side of the river, and the Buda Hills beyond. I also visited the Treasury museum, where an early 1900s oil sketch by Hungarian artist Gyula Benczúr — designer of the mosaics above the cathedral's main altar — was a highlight. Inside the cathedral's nave, the mummified hand of St Stephen, displayed in an ornate replica of the building, was a fascinating discovery. ABC News chief medical correspondent Dr. Tara Narula joined "Good Morning America" on Wednesday to discuss a new study that suggests GLP-1 medications may be linked to a reduced risk of developing breast cancer . The study, which was published in the JCO Oncology Practice journal, looked at University of Pennsylvania Health System records from more than 111,000 women ages 45 to 80 over the last several years who were overweight or obese, to see who went on to develop breast cancer. "They found that those women on GLP[-1]s had a reduced risk of developing breast cancer by about 30%," Narula explained Wednesday. Narula discussed the potential links between GLP-1s and breast cancer, explaining that after menopause , fat cells produce estrogen throughout the body, and higher levels of estrogen could translate to a higher risk of breast cancer. Entry-level workers "have to be focused on ensuring that they are actually building critical thinking [and] judgment," Nair tells CNBC Make It. In an IBM survey of 1,500 chief human resources officers and 8,800 employees worldwide published in September, roughly 57% of CHROs considered critical thinking an important skill in the AI era, compared to 49% of employees. items.text: Ex-Meta Executive Who Now Runs $1 Billion Firm Shares Mark Zuckerberg’s Work-Life Balance Lesson
items.article: A former Meta executive who worked closely with Mark Zuckerberg says one lesson from his time at Facebook changed how he thinks about work, leadership and the value of time. Working long hours may seem like part of building a successful company, but former Meta executive Martin Ott says his time working with Mark Zuckerberg taught him a different approach. Ott, who is now the CEO of Berlin-based tax platform Taxfix, says leaders should focus on the work that matters most instead of trying to stay busy all day. Taxfix is valued at more than $1 billion. Ott joined Facebook in 2012 as managing director for Northern and Central Europe. The company was still private at the time and was moving from desktop use to mobile, with only a few thousand employees around the world. Speaking to Fortune, Ott said one of the key lessons he took from working under Zuckerberg was that time is limited and should be used carefully. “There’s only so many hours in a day," Ott said. Ott Says Leaders Should Focus On One Key Task Rather than filling the day with meetings and tasks, Ott believes leaders should think about what could have the biggest effect on the business. “Ask yourself, what is the real one thing you could do today to really have impact, make a difference?" he said. He also suggested that employees and managers should think twice before joining every meeting on their calendars. According to Ott, spending more hours at work does not always mean creating more value.

items.article: Amanda Peet had an early breast cancer warning sign six months before she was diagnosed. She reveals the skin symptom that she calls “weird.” It wasn’t a lump. Amanda Peet was diagnosed with breast cancer last fall, but she had an early warning sign that something was wrong six months earlier. The actor revealed the “weird” symptom during an interview with TODAY on Thursday, Oct. 1. “I was in my closet, I was probably putting something on and I felt a weird — it just didn’t feel like normal skin, but it wasn’t the frozen pea that everybody talks about,” Peet, 54, told Savannah Guthrie, referring to what a breast cancer lump can feel like. “I went and I even got an MRI and then they sent me away. So I thought I had a clean bill of health, but they were actually watching it.” Six months later, on the Friday before Labor Day in 2025, the actor thought she was going in for a routine scan, when her doctor spotted something concerning on her ultrasound, Peet wrote in an essay for The New Yorker . She knew something was wrong because her physician, who was usually very chatty, went silent. The doctor then performed a biopsy and told her she would walk the sample over to Cedars-Sinai and hand-deliver it on a Friday night, another concerning clue.

items.article: A Colorado man's unusual commute to work is catching the attention of tens of thousands online. Jake Hutzler, an air traffic controller, travels to his job site at Pueblo Memorial Airport by power paragliding at least once a week and shares his flying adventures on Instagram. "There's nothing better than flying to work, you know, 500 feet in the air, sipping your coffee," Hutzler told ABC News' Danny New . While he's soaring through the sky, Hutzler says he likes to sip coffee and even eat breakfast, like a burrito. The father of one said paragliding from his home to the airport takes about the same time as driving a car -- about 20 minutes, but if he catches a good tailwind, he can shave his travel time down to 15 minutes or less. "It's probably the closest thing that you can get to a jetpack," said Hutzler. To power paraglide, Hutzler wears an engine propeller backpack called a paramotor, which can typically cost between $8,000 and $9,000.

Updated October 1, 2026 — 3:07pm , first published 3:00pm You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Before 33-year-old Chontaine Adair was diagnosed with stage 4 metastatic breast cancer in 2025, she had a very different perception of the disease. “I just didn’t think it could happen at my age, and I had a mindset that it couldn’t happen to me,” says Adair, who is based in Sydney. This misconception, says the mother of two, was partly shaped by age-specific cancer-screening advice. “I didn’t know anyone in their early thirties with breast cancer, and any ads regarding checks like mammograms, for example, show older women and even mention, ‘If you are [a certain] age, get tested’, and this age was always older.
